extracted.intended_audience: geometers, mathematical researchers and advanced students interested in classical geometry, conic sections, and the history of solutions to inscription/circumscription problems
extracted.subtask_description: A historical survey and critical review of methods and solutions for the classical problem of inscribing/circumscribing polygons with prescribed incidence/tangency conditions (circles and conics). It summarizes geometric and analytic approaches, points out omissions, special/indeterminate cases, and methodological lessons for future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature check and proper attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify prior publications and acknowledge earlier investigators before asserting novelty (e.g., Lowry finding Simson's treatment after his own discovery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rebuts an unfair charge of plagiarism by pointing out that a prior work (Simson's Opera Reliqua) contains a full investigation; advice implicit: turn to earlier volumes and sources before making imputation of originality or plagiarism. Be cautious about claiming novelty without checking contemporaneous and earlier sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle and report special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly consider special or degenerate cases in constructions and proofs (example: when a circle is reduced to a point aligned with three other points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes: 'No notice however is taken of special cases: more particularly of that, when the circle is reduced to a point situated in the same line with the other three.' Authors should note and treat such special cases rather than omit them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and directness of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor constructions that are 'remarkably simple and direct' where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises Lowry's construction as 'remarkably simple and direct'; this is a positive evaluative criterion—prefer methods that achieve the result with minimal and transparent steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conjecture from proved generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer broad generalizations from a single or limited case; ensure the general statement is demonstrated rather than conjectured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As observed about Simson: 'There is nothing in the structure of the analysis itself that suggests the investigation to be adapted to the higher values of n... We have no right therefore to infer that the generalised statement was ... demonstration as of probable conjecture.' Authors should provide proof when asserting generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use projective principles to generalize circle results to conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt projective methods to extend constructions/theorems from the circle to general conic sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes that 'by the adoption of the projective principle, the conic section generally might be substituted for the circle'—recommend employing projective geometry to obtain wider applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate (analytic) methods are legitimate but can be laborious
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartesian/coordinate approaches are valid ways to solve inscription/circumscription problems, though calculations may be lengthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearn and Gaskin's coordinate solutions are recognized as successful; the text remarks 'The calculations required are extremely laborious, but always of the most simple kind.' Use coordinates when appropriate, but expect heavy algebraic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide geometric proofs for propositions used in geometric arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proposition (especially projective or polar properties) is used in a geometric context, furnish a geometric demonstration rather than rely solely on citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author objected to Gaskin's use of a quoted proposition 'except he gave a geometrical demonstration of it; and he furnished me with one rigidly so.' If invoking a nontrivial proposition, include a geometric proof or clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to dual problems when helpful (inscription ↔ circumscription)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform problems to their dual form (e.g., circumscription instead of inscription) to simplify analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearn 'reduces the problem of the inscription to its dual, of circumscription'—this methodological step can make equations and constructions more tractable and should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat indeterminate and ambiguous cases with care
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise great caution when applying general principles to special data relations: results may become illusory, porismatic, indeterminate, or inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote: 'Great caution is, however, necessary in the application of a general principle to special cases where particular relations subsist amongst the data. The expression may become illusory; the construction porismatic; the theorem indeterminate, doubly or triply; or the process itself be excluded...' Authors must analyze degenerate or exceptional configurations explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce and use reciprocal polars for higher-order inscribed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ the doctrine of reciprocal polars to describe figures beyond triangles and to obtain general constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes the 'doctrine of reciprocal polars' is 'directly brought into play, for the first time, for the description of any figure beyond the triangle.' Use this tool for general polygon-conic interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constructive (poristic) analyses that hold even when the polygon does not close
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that investigate inscribed properties irrespective of the polygon 'closing' (i.e., poristic analysis) are valuable and often more robust than analyses that assume existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find loci/lines that yield multiple solutions (handle multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When problems admit multiple solutions (e.g., two inscribed polygons), derive the locus or equation (line) whose intersections give the different solution positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaskin 'was led to the happy thought of finding the equation of the line in which the corresponding vertices of the two solutional triangles were situated; and hence by constructing this line, its intersections with the curve give the two positions...' When multiplicity arises, look for such global constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply anharmonic ratio and projective invariants for envelopes and Poncelet constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the anharmonic ratio and other projective invariants to investigate envelopes (free side locus) and to demonstrate Poncelet-type constructions succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Townsend's application of the anharmonic ratio 'to investigate the envelope of the free side, and to establish the truth of Poncelet’s construction' is singled out as notable—projective invariants can yield concise, powerful proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about possible omissions and limits of survey
rubrics_metrics.description: State transparently when literature searches may be incomplete and limit conclusions to the solutions actually examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's remark: 'Although I have bestowed adequate care in the examination of those books to which I could obtain access, I still feel a suspicion of something having escaped my search.' When surveying history, acknowledge gaps and defer to later workers to fill chasms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value elegance and pedagogical clarity in published solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegant, strictly geometrical solutions that can serve as models for students are especially valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praises such as 'exceedingly elegant and strictly geometrical' and the intention to print solutions 'as models for the undergraduates' indicate a preference for clear, instructive expositions suitable for teaching and further study.
